newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU cautious about Thomson cash injection.
newsitem.headline: EU cautious about Thomson cash injection.

text.p: European Commission officials reacted cautiously to the announcement on Wednesday of a 11 billion French franc ($2.1 billion) capital injection into Thomson SA before privatisation.

But they warned that the Commission would have to assess the proposed recapitalisation of the state-owned defence and consumer electronics group under European Union rules designed to control state subsidies to businesses.
"This is a very sensitive case," a Commission official started by saying when asked whether the Commission had been notified of the French government.
The official hinted Paris had already sounded out the Commission on the issue, but declined to elaborate.
The French government said on Wednesday it had chosen to sell Thomson SA to Lagardere Groupe, which together with Alcatel Alsthom SA had put in bids for the loss-making company.

If approved by France's Independent Privatisation Commission, the sale itself will most certainly have to be examined under the European Union's merger rules which ban creation or strengthening of dominant positions, another Commission official said. However, the EU may only be notified of the civilan aspects of the sale, as national governments are allowed to retain information that affects their defence interests.
Paris also said that it would pump 11 billion francs into Thomson, which is a leading maker of televisions, as well as a specialist in defence electronics such as missile guidance sustems.
Under EU state aid rules, all state injections or any other public financial support to ailing businesses must be approved by the Commission before they become effective.
When the company is state-controlled, the Commission must assess whether the government carrying the cash injection is acting like any other private investor would.
If this is the case, the plan goes through.
But if the market-investor test fails, the Commission sees that the subsidies are limited to the strict minimum needed and do not distort fair competition.
It may even ask how much the two rival bidders offered for Thomson, to see whether the French government picked up the higher offer.
The Commission openly questioned in the past plans to help the restructuring and privatisation of ailing companies.

This includes the privatisation of SKET, Germany's heavy machinery giant, where it said the purchasers had not shared any of the financial burden. It also contested that the restructuring plan guaranteed the company's return to profitability. Sket's sale aborted and the Commission is still examining the issue. -- Amelia Torres 322 2876841 ($ = 5.208 French Francs)
